intro-1.text: How firing *alpha particles* at gold revealed the *nucleus* at the heart of every atom
intro-1.say: The gold foil experiment. How firing alpha particles at a sheet of gold revealed the nucleus, at the heart of every atom.

electron-1.text: In 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the *electron*: a tiny particle with *negative charge*
electron-1.say: In eighteen ninety-seven, J. J. Thomson discovered the electron: a tiny particle with negative charge.

electron-2.text: But atoms are *neutral* overall. So where was the *positive charge* hiding?

plum-2.text: The atom is a sphere about *10⁻¹⁰ m* across, with positive charge *spread evenly* through it
plum-2.say: The atom is a sphere about ten to the minus ten metres across, with positive charge spread evenly through it.

plum-3.text: Electrons sit inside like *seeds in a watermelon*, so the atom stays neutral

plum-4.text: Spread that thin, the positive charge pushes weakly, so alpha particles should *pass straight through*

alpha-1.text: Rutherford himself had discovered *alpha particles*, in 1899
alpha-1.say: Rutherford himself had discovered alpha particles, in eighteen ninety-nine.

alpha-2.text: Each one is a *helium nucleus*: two protons and two neutrons, with charge *+2e*
alpha-2.say: Each one is a helium nucleus: two protons and two neutrons, with a charge of plus two e.

alpha-3.text: They shoot out of radioactive atoms at about *20,000 km/s*, carrying a few *MeV* of energy
alpha-3.say: They shoot out of radioactive atoms at about twenty thousand kilometres per second, carrying a few million electron volts of energy.

alpha-4.text: Fast, heavy and positive: *perfect tiny bullets* for probing the atom

setup-1.text: In 1909, Hans *Geiger* and Ernest *Marsden*, working under Rutherford, built this experiment
setup-1.say: In nineteen oh nine, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, working under Rutherford, built this experiment.

setup-2.text: A radioactive source sits in a *lead block*. Lead absorbs radiation, so only a *narrow beam* escapes

setup-3.text: The beam strikes *gold foil* about *100 nm* thick: only a few hundred atoms
setup-3.say: The beam strikes gold foil about a hundred nanometres thick: only a few hundred atoms.

setup-4.text: Gold was chosen because it can be beaten *incredibly thin*

setup-5.text: A *zinc sulfide* screen gives a tiny *flash of light* wherever an alpha particle lands

setup-6.text: A *microscope* swings round the foil, so they can count flashes *at every angle*

setup-7.text: And it all sits in a *vacuum*, so air doesn't stop the alpha particles

fire-1.text: Here's what they saw. *Most* alpha particles went *straight through*, as if nothing was there

fire-2.text: A small fraction were *deflected*: about *1 in 700* by more than a degree
fire-2.say: A small fraction were deflected: about one in seven hundred, by more than a degree.

fire-3.text: And some *bounced back*: about *1 in 8000* by more than *90°*
fire-3.say: And some bounced back: about one in eight thousand, by more than ninety degrees.

quote-1.say: Rutherford said: It was almost as incredible as if you fired a fifteen-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper, and it came back and hit you.

graph-1.text: Plot the *number* of alpha particles against the *scattering angle*, and the count falls off steeply

graph-2.text: Rutherford's formula fits it perfectly: *N ∝ 1 / sin⁴(θ/2)*
graph-2.say: Rutherford's formula fits it perfectly: N is proportional to one over sine to the fourth of theta over two.

graph-3.text: That's exactly what happens if all the positive charge sits at a *single tiny point*

inside-1.text: Zoom into the foil, and we reach rows of *gold atoms*

inside-2.text: Each atom is mostly *empty space*, so most particles fly straight through

inside-3.text: But all its positive charge, and nearly all its *mass*, is packed into a tiny *nucleus*

inside-4.text: How far a particle's path is aimed from the nucleus is the *impact parameter, b*

inside-5.text: Large *b*: a tiny deflection. Small *b*: a big one

inside-6.text: Head on, with *b = 0*, the alpha particle stops and *bounces straight back*
inside-6.say: Head on, with b equal to zero, the alpha particle stops, and bounces straight back.

closest-1.text: How close can it get? Head on, all its *kinetic energy* turns into *electric potential energy*

closest-2.text: At the *distance of closest approach, d*, the two are equal

closest-3.say: K equals two Z e squared, over four pi epsilon nought d. So, d equals two Z e squared, over four pi epsilon nought K.

closest-4.text: For a *7.7 MeV* alpha particle and gold, *Z = 79*: d ≈ *3 × 10⁻¹⁴ m*
closest-4.say: For a seven point seven M e V alpha particle and gold, with Z equal to seventy-nine, d is about three times ten to the minus fourteen metres.

closest-5.text: So the nucleus must be *even smaller* than that

scale-1.text: Later measurements put the nucleus at about *10⁻¹⁵ m*: a *hundred thousand times* smaller than the atom
scale-1.say: Later measurements put the nucleus at about ten to the minus fifteen metres: a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom.

scale-2.text: If the nucleus were a *cricket ball*, the atom would have a radius of about *5 km*
scale-2.say: If the nucleus were a cricket ball, the atom would have a radius of about five kilometres.

model-1.text: This led to Rutherford's *nuclear model* of the atom, in 1911
model-1.say: This led to Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom, in nineteen eleven.

model-2.text: One: a tiny, dense, *positive nucleus* holds almost all the atom's mass

model-3.text: Two: *electrons* move around it in circular orbits, like *planets* around the sun

model-4.text: The nucleus's *electrostatic pull* provides the *centripetal force*

model-5.text: Three: the atom is *neutral*, with as many electrons as protons

limits-1.text: But the model had a serious flaw. An electron moving in a circle is *accelerating*

limits-2.text: And *accelerating charges radiate* energy, as electromagnetic waves

limits-3.text: Losing energy, it would *spiral into the nucleus* in about *10⁻⁸ s*. Atoms would collapse. They don't
limits-3.say: Losing energy, it would spiral into the nucleus in about a hundred millionth of a second. Atoms would collapse. They don't.

limits-4.text: It also can't explain *line spectra*: why atoms emit only *certain colours*, not a continuous rainbow

outro-1.text: To sum up: the atom is mostly *empty space*, with a tiny, dense, *positive nucleus* at its centre

outro-2.text: Fixing the model's flaws led *Niels Bohr*, in 1913, to a new model of the atom. But that's another story
outro-2.say: Fixing the model's flaws led Niels Bohr, in nineteen thirteen, to a new model of the atom. But that's another story.
